div.head: IV Eg Prolog
div.ab: ✠ Her is geswutelod on þisum gewrite, hu Eadgar cyningc wæs smeagende, hwæt to bote mihte æt ðæm færcwealme, ðe his leodscipe swyðe drehte ⁊ wanode wide gynd his anweald.
Her is geswutelod on þisum gewrite, hu Eadgar cyncg wæs smeagende, hwæt to bote mihte æt þam færcwealme, þe his leodscype swyðe drehte ⁊ wanode wide gynd his anweald.

In huius litterature continetur serie, quemadmodum rex inclitus Eadgar diligenter cępit perquirere et inuestigare, quid ad remedium ualeret incommoditati publicę, morti scilicet subitanee, que suam longe latéque patriam uexabat graui peste.
Her is geswutelod on þisum gewrite, hu Eadgar cyncg wæs smeagende, hwæt to bote mihte æt þam færcwealme þe his leodscype swyðe drehte ⁊ wanode, wide gynd his anweald.

IV Eg. Prol. ✠ Hier in dieser Urkunde ist kundgethan, wie König Eadgar berieth, was zur Besserung [dienen] könnte bei dem plötzlichen Sterben, welches sein Volk sehr quälte und verminderte weithin über sein Gebiet.

IV Eg. Prologue. ✠ Here in this document it is made known how King Edgar considered what might [serve] as a remedy for the sudden mortality which greatly afflicted his people and diminished it far and wide throughout his dominion.

Notification is hereby given in this order, that King Eadgar has been considering what remedy could be found for the plague which has greatly afflicted and reduced his people throughout the length and breadth of his dominion.
✠Here it is made known in this document how King Edgar inquired what could be a remedy in the sudden pestilence which greatly oppressed and reduced his people far and wide throughout his dominion.

This is the style of a charter (see that word in Gl 1), which is what the document calls itself once more at 15, 1; thus Æthelred II’s charter begins: Her swutelað on þison gewrite, hu Æ. kyning; Earle Landchar. 217; similarly Thorpe Dipl. 312. 320. 586. 610

This beginning is common in wills and other A.S. documents of the tenth and eleventh centuries, see Kemble, Nos. 429, 591, 593, 594, 738, 745 etc.
Cf. Sax. Chr. ann. 962 A, where a plague and a great fire in London are recorded.

This interesting code, which throws light on how the statutes were circulated and on Edgar’s relations with the Danelaw, survives in Old English in B.L.Cott. Nero E. i, probably from Worcester, and both in Old English and Latin in C.C.C.C., MS. 265, which contains Wulfstan’s writings and materials. It is not in Quadripartitus. The code has also a stylistic interest, for it departs from the succinct, often obscure, style of earlier legal documents, and affords an example of a homiletic style before the period of the great homilists Ælfric and Wulfstan. It is tempting to connect it with one of the great churchmen who surrounded King Edgar. The code seems especially directed to the Danish areas, Northumbria, East Anglia, and part of Mercia; chap. 14 implies that separate regulations had been drawn up for English areas. The archbishop in chap. 1.4 is presumably Dunstan of Canterbury; only Northumbria and part of the north Midlands were in the province of York. The plague which occasioned the issue of these injunctions is likely to be that entered in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 962 ‘A’. A date soon after that is consonant with what is known of the persons mentioned in the code. The text is edited by Liebermann, I, 206–15; and with English translation, by Robertson, pp. 28–39, Thorpe, I, 270–9.
